title: Containers on AWS: ECS, EKS, and Fargate

questions.prompt: How does a container differ from a virtual machine?

options.text: A container shares the host OS kernel (lightweight); a VM runs its own full OS
A container runs its own full OS; a VM shares the host kernel

questions.explanation: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full OS each; a container virtualizes the OS and shares the host kernel as an isolated process, making it lighter and faster to start.

options.text: A serverless compute engine that runs containers without you managing EC2 servers

questions.explanation: Fargate runs containers serverlessly — no EC2 cluster to provision or patch — and works with both ECS and EKS.

questions.prompt: When should you choose Amazon EKS over Amazon ECS?

options.text: When you specifically need the Kubernetes standard, ecosystem, or portability

questions.explanation: ECS is simpler and AWS-native; EKS is managed Kubernetes with more complexity, chosen when you need the Kubernetes API, ecosystem, or cross-cloud portability.

questions.prompt: Match each AWS service to its role with containers.
questions.explanation: ECR stores images, ECS is the AWS-native orchestrator, EKS is managed Kubernetes, and Fargate provides serverless compute for containers.

questions.prompt: Managing many containers across hosts — scheduling, scaling, and healing them — is called container ____.
questions.explanation: Orchestration handles scheduling, scaling, restarting, and networking many containers; ECS and EKS are orchestrators.

questions.prompt: A small team needs a simple always-on microservice with minimal ops and no Kubernetes requirement. What's a sensible choice?

options.text: ECS with the Fargate launch type
EKS with a self-managed cluster, because Kubernetes is popular
A single Lambda with a 40-minute timeout

questions.explanation: ECS + Fargate runs the containerized service with no servers to manage and no Kubernetes complexity — the simplest fit when Kubernetes isn't required.
